unit.title: States and properties of matter
unit.blurb: Gases, the three states of water, evaporation, condensation and dissolving.

O1.t: Describe gases using the particle model and name oxygen and carbon dioxide.

O2.t: Describe water as a solid, liquid and gas, and know its melting point (0 °C) and boiling point (100 °C).

O3.t: Describe evaporation and condensation and explain the water cycle.

O4.t: Investigate what makes evaporation faster and use measurements to draw a conclusion.

O5.t: Describe dissolving, solutions, soluble and insoluble substances, and how to get a solute back.

captions: Hello, matter masters! Take a deep breath… in… and out.
This is lesson 3.1: gases.
You just breathed in a gas called air. You cannot see it, but it is all around you.
Air fills balloons, footballs, bubbles, and even the tiny holes in a sponge. Air is real stuff!
Everything is made of tiny particles.
In a solid, the particles are packed tightly. In a liquid, they slide around.
In a gas, they zoom about, far apart, in every direction. That is why a gas spreads out to fill any space.
Pause and think. Why does a gas spread out to fill its container?
Here is a tasty example. Someone opens a pizza box in the kitchen.
Tiny particles of smelly gas spread out through the air.
A few seconds later, they reach your nose in the living room. Yum! Gases spread out.
Air is a mixture of gases. Oxygen is the gas we breathe in. Every living thing needs it.
Carbon dioxide is the gas we breathe out. It also makes the bubbles in fizzy drinks.
Helium is lighter than air, so helium balloons float up, up and away!
Did you know? Air has mass, so it has weight.
Weigh a flat football, then pump it up and weigh it again. It is heavier! The air inside adds a few grams.
Your turn. Which gas do we breathe out?
Let's find hidden air.
Put some dry soil in a clear jar, and slowly pour water over it.
Watch closely. Can you see bubbles rising?
The bubbles are air that was hiding between the bits of soil.
Let's remember.
Air is a mixture of gases.
In a gas, the particles are far apart and move very fast.
So gases spread out to fill any space.
We breathe in oxygen, and breathe out carbon dioxide.
Gas-tastic work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, water wizards! Splash!
This is lesson 3.2: properties of water.
Water is amazing, because we can find it in all three states.
As a solid, it is ice.
As a liquid, it is the water we drink.
And as a gas, it is invisible water vapour.
Meet an ice lolly. In the freezer, it is a hard solid.
Take it out into the sunshine, and it starts to melt. Drip, drip!
Soon it is a sticky puddle of liquid.
Put the liquid back in the freezer, and it freezes into a solid again. Melting and freezing are reversible changes.
Pause and think. At what temperature does ice melt?
Ice melts at zero degrees Celsius. Water freezes at zero degrees too.
If we heat water to one hundred degrees Celsius, it boils. Big bubbles of water vapour form inside it.
That is why a kettle makes so much steam. Always ask an adult, because steam can burn.
Water has some special properties. It flows, and takes the shape of its container.
Lots of things dissolve in water, like salt and sugar.
And here is a strange one. Ice floats on water! Most solids sink in their own liquid, but not ice.
Did you know? Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top down.
The ice is like a lid, and the fish keep swimming in the water underneath all winter.
Your turn. At what temperature does water boil?
Let's have an ice cube race!
Put the same size ice cube in different places: a sunny window, a shady room and the fridge.
Time how long each ice cube takes to melt completely.
Where does ice melt fastest? Predict first, then test!
Let's remember.
Water can be solid ice, liquid water, or water vapour gas.
Ice melts, and water freezes, at zero degrees Celsius.
Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
And ice floats on water.
Wonderful wizardry! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, weather watchers! Where does a puddle go? Let's find out.
This is lesson 3.3: evaporation and condensation.
After the rain, there is a big puddle in the playground.
Then the sun comes out, and warms the water.
Slowly, the water turns into invisible water vapour and rises into the air. This is evaporation.
By home time, the puddle has vanished. Mystery solved!
Pause and think. What is evaporation?
What makes washing dry faster? Warmth helps water evaporate faster.
Wind helps too, because it carries the water vapour away.
And spreading the washing out gives a bigger surface, so more water can evaporate.
Now the opposite. Take a cold drink from the fridge, and wait a few minutes.
Little drops of water appear on the outside of the glass! Water vapour in the air cooled down on the cold glass and turned back into a liquid. This is condensation.
You can spot condensation everywhere. A bathroom mirror goes steamy after a hot shower.
Car windows get misty on a cold morning.
And on a cold day, you can see your own breath, as tiny drops of condensed water!
Evaporation and condensation make the water cycle.
The sun warms the sea, and water evaporates.
High in the sky, the water vapour cools and condenses into clouds.
When the drops get heavy, they fall as rain, and flow back to the sea. Round and round, for ever!
Your turn. How does a cloud form?
Let's test evaporation.
Wet three identical cloths with the same amount of water.
Hang one in the sun, one in the shade, and one indoors. Weigh them every thirty minutes.
The cloth that gets lightest fastest lost the most water by evaporation.
Let's remember.
Evaporation is when a liquid turns into a gas.
Warmth, wind and a bigger surface make it faster.
Condensation is when a gas turns back into a liquid, on a cold surface.
And together they make the water cycle.
Super scientists! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, kitchen chemists! Pass me a spoon.
This is lesson 3.4: solutions.
Stir a spoon of sugar into warm water. Watch it disappear!
But taste the water. It is sweet, so the sugar is still there. It has dissolved: its particles have spread out between the water particles.
A liquid with something dissolved in it is called a solution.
Pause and think. What is a solution?
Let's test some things. Salt dissolves in water. It is soluble.
Instant coffee dissolves too. Soluble!
Sand does not dissolve. It just sinks to the bottom. Sand is insoluble.
Oil does not dissolve either. It floats on top in a shiny layer.
How can we make sugar dissolve faster? Use warmer water, because the particles move faster.
Stirring helps too, and so do smaller pieces. Sugar dissolves faster than a sugar cube.
Riddle time! I can disappear in water, but I am still there. You can taste me in the sea. What am I?
Salt!
Dissolving can be reversed. Leave salty water in a warm, sunny place.
The water evaporates, but the salt cannot. Salt crystals are left behind. This is how people make sea salt!
Your turn. How can you get salt back from salty water?
Let's have a sugar race.
Pour the same amount of water into three cups: cold, warm and hot. Ask an adult to help.
Add one spoon of sugar to each cup, and stir the same way.
Time how long the sugar takes to dissolve. Which wins?
Let's remember.
When something dissolves, its particles spread out in the liquid.
Soluble things dissolve, and insoluble things do not.
Warmth and stirring make dissolving faster.
And evaporating the water gets the solid back.
Excellent chemistry! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

steps: Pour the same amount of cold, warm and hot water into the three cups.
Add one level teaspoon of sugar to the cold water, stir and start the timer.
Stop the timer when you cannot see any sugar.
